extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates or graduate students studying algebraic geometry (readers of Vakil's Foundations)
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, criteria, and constructions relating Weil and Cartier divisors, invertible sheaves (line bundles), class groups/Picard groups, and the correspondence between graded modules and quasicoherent sheaves on Proj; plus notions of global generation and maps to projective space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal divisor
rubrics_metrics.description: D is principal if D = div f for some rational function f. Principal divisors form a subgroup Prin X; div induces a group homomorphism K(X)× → Prin X.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principal divisors are exactly those coming from a single rational function; record that Prin X is a subgroup of Weil X and that principal divisors are the image of the div map from K(X)×.

rubrics_metrics.name: Locally principal divisor
rubrics_metrics.description: D is locally principal if X can be covered with open sets Ui such that on each Ui the restriction of D is principal. LocPrin X denotes the subgroup of locally principal divisors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being locally principal is weaker than being globally principal; LocPrin X is the natural domain for constructing invertible sheaves OX(D).

rubrics_metrics.name: Invertibility criterion via local principality
rubrics_metrics.description: If D is locally principal (and X is normal Noetherian), then OX(D) is locally isomorphic to OX, i.e., OX(D) is an invertible sheaf.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation 14.2.5: principal divisors give O(D) ≅ O; conversely (diagram (14.2.7.1) and Exercise 14.2.G) if O(D) is invertible then D is locally principal. Thus local principality ↔ invertibility of O(D).

rubrics_metrics.name: Isomorphism O(div s) ≅ L via a rational section
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an invertible sheaf L and a nonzero rational section s of L, there is an isomorphism O(div s) ∼= L obtained by sending a rational function t (with zeros/poles constrained by div s) to the rational section st.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct on opens U where O(div s)|U ≅ OU: define φU : O(div s)(U) → L(U) by t ↦ s·t, show φU is an isomorphism and glue; choose it so that the canonical σ satisfies σ(1)=s (Exercise 14.2.E and (b)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Canonical section σ(1) detects divisor
rubrics_metrics.description: If OX(D) is invertible, then div(σ(1)) = D where σ(1) is the canonical rational section defined in the construction of OX(D); conversely this property characterizes locally principal divisors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise 14.2.G: part (a) shows the equality div(σ(1)) = D; part (b) gives the converse — this ties the sheaf construction and the divisor back together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting non-locally-principal Weil divisors
rubrics_metrics.description: A Weil divisor may fail to be locally principal; e.g., on the cone X = Spec k[x,y,z]/(xy − z^2) the line D given by z=x=0 is not locally principal (inspect stalk at the origin and use Zariski tangent space).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To show a divisor is not locally principal, analyze local rings/stalks (e.g., failure of a single local equation) and tangent-space/invariant arguments as in Exercise 14.2.H.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factorial (UFD) implies O(D) invertible
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is Noetherian and factorial (Spec of a UFD), then for any Weil divisor D, O(D) is an invertible sheaf; consequently Pic X → Cl X is an isomorphism (Proposition 14.2.10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use that in a UFD all codimension-1 primes are principal (Lemma 11.1.6), so every Weil divisor is locally principal; therefore O(D) are line bundles and class group vanishes on Spec of a UFD.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class group and Picard group relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Class group Cl X is defined as Weil X / Prin X. There is an inclusion Pic X ↪ Cl X (coming from mapping invertible sheaves to Weil divisors), summarized in diagram (14.2.7.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand the exact relationships in the diagram: invertible sheaves with sections map to locally principal divisors, mod out principal divisors to obtain the class group; interpret examples (e.g., Pic P^n ≅ Z generated by O(1)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Excision exact sequence for class groups
rubrics_metrics.description: If Z is an irreducible codimension-1 subset of X, there is an exact sequence 0 → Z[Z] → Weil X → Weil(X − Z) → 0; on class groups this yields Z → Cl X → Cl(X − Z) → 0 (possibly losing exactness on the left).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removing closed subsets of codimension >1 doesn't change Weil divisor group or principal divisors, but removing codimension-1 loci changes class groups in a controllable way (Exercise 14.2.8 and example computations).

rubrics_metrics.name: UFD characterization via class group
rubrics_metrics.description: A Noetherian integral domain A is a UFD if and only if A is integrally closed and Cl Spec A = 0 (Exercise 14.2.T).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One direction: UFD ⇒ integrally closed and codimension-1 primes principal ⇒ Cl = 0. For the converse use characterization that codimension-1 primes principal implies UFD and tools such as Algebraic Hartogs (Lemma 11.3.11).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nagata's Lemma for UFD
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is Noetherian and x ∈ A is such that (x) is prime and A[1/x] is a UFD, then A is a UFD (Exercise 14.2.U).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the short exact sequence relating class groups (14.2.8.1) to deduce Cl Spec A = 0 and check integrally closedness via analysis of integral dependence after inverting x.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective Cartier divisor (ideal-sheaf criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A closed subscheme D ⊂ X is an effective Cartier divisor iff its ideal sheaf I_D is an invertible sheaf (equivalently, locally cut out by a single non-zerodivisor); in the locally Noetherian case this is 'locally cut out by one equation not vanishing at any associated point'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives multiple equivalent characterizations: invertible ideal sheaf ⇔ locally principal ideal generated by a non-zerodivisor ⇔ scheme locally cut out by one equation with no associated-point vanishing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invertible sheaf associated to an effective Cartier divisor
rubrics_metrics.description: For an effective Cartier divisor D, define O(D) := (I_D)^∨ (the dual of the ideal sheaf); then I_D = O(−D) and there is the exact sequence 0 → O(−D) → O → O_D → 0 and a canonical section s_D of O(D) cutting out D.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dualization choice (rather than taking I_D itself) ensures the canonical section behaves as expected; check Exercise 14.3.B and 14.3.C for verifying the section cuts out D.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence: section not a zerodivisor ⇔ effective Cartier divisor
rubrics_metrics.description: If L is an invertible sheaf and s ∈ Γ(X, L) is a section that is locally not a zerodivisor (i.e., does not vanish at any associated point), then s = 0 cuts out an effective Cartier divisor D and O(D) ≅ L; conversely s_D for an effective Cartier divisor is not a zerodivisor and cuts out D.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives the correspondence between pairs (L, s) with s locally not a zerodivisor and effective Cartier divisors; see Exercises 14.3.C and 14.3.D for the constructions and verifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Products and sums of Cartier divisors
rubrics_metrics.description: If I and J are invertible ideal sheaves corresponding to effective Cartier divisors D and D', then their product IJ is an invertible ideal sheaf corresponding to D + D', and O(D + D') ≅ O(D) ⊗ O(D').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define product of quasicoherent ideals locally by usual ideal multiplication and verify compatibility under localization; the divisor semigroup corresponds to tensor product of associated line bundles (Exercise 14.3.E).

rubrics_metrics.name: Functor from graded modules to quasicoherent sheaves on Proj
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a graded S-module M, the construction M ↦ ˜M defines a quasicoherent sheaf on Proj S by ˜M|_{D(f)} = (M_f)_0 (the degree-0 piece after localizing at homogeneous f). This functor is exact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The construction glues on distinguished opens D(f) using the degree-0 pieces; Exercise 15.1.B: the functor ∼ is exact. Note: the functor is not an equivalence of categories (Exercise 15.1.C) but is close in behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and properties of O(n) on Proj
rubrics_metrics.description: If S is a graded ring, define O_Proj S(n) (abbreviated O(n)) by ˜S(n). If S is generated in degree 1, then O(n) is an invertible sheaf, global sections Γ(Proj S, O(n)) are homogeneous degree-n elements of S, and O(m+n) ≅ O(m) ⊗ O(n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use shifts of graded modules M(n)_m = M_{n+m} to produce twists; when S ≅ A[x0,...,xm] one recovers the standard O(n) on P^m with homogeneous polynomials as global sections (Exercises 15.2.A–D).

rubrics_metrics.name: Globally generated (generated by global sections)
rubrics_metrics.description: A quasicoherent sheaf F on X is globally generated if there exists a surjection O_X^{⊕I} → F (for some index set I). F is finitely globally generated if I can be taken finite. F is globally generated at p if the map is surjective on stalks at p.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalent condition for finite-type F: F globally generated at p iff the map Γ(X,F) → F_p / m_p F_p is surjective (geometric Nakayama, Exercise 15.3.C(a)). Global generation can be checked on stalks and can be localized near points (Exercise 15.3.C(b)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Local-to-global criteria for generation
rubrics_metrics.description: If F is finite type and X quasicompact, then F is globally generated iff it is generated by finitely many global sections; if F is generated at all closed points of a quasicompact scheme then F is globally generated everywhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use finiteness hypotheses and existence of closed points in quasicompact schemes (Exercises 15.3.C and 15.3.D) to pass from local fiber-generation to global generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Base locus and base-point-free line bundles
rubrics_metrics.description: For an invertible sheaf L, the base locus is the closed set of points where all global sections of L vanish; L is base-point-free (equivalently globally generated) if this locus is empty. Tensor product of base-point-free line bundles is base-point-free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For line bundles, global generation ⇔ for every point p there exists a global section not vanishing at p (Exercise 15.3.E). The base locus can be refined to a scheme-theoretic intersection of vanishing loci of all sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sections giving maps to projective space
rubrics_metrics.description: Given n+1 global sections s0,...,sn of an invertible sheaf L with no common zero, they define a morphism X → P^n by x ↦ [s0(x):...:sn(x)], constructed locally via trivializations and shown to glue (Exercise 15.3.F).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the standard correspondence between base-point-free linear systems and morphisms to projective space; check independence from trivialization and glue compatibility using basic facts about morphisms determined by n+1 functions with no common zeros (Exercise 6.3.M referenced).

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation of coherent sheaves on Proj by O(−n)
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem 15.3.1: any finite type quasicoherent sheaf F on Proj S (S finitely generated over A, generated in degree 1) admits a presentation by a finite direct sum of twists of O(−n): ⊕_finite O(−n) → F → 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This gives concrete control over coherent sheaves on projective schemes and is the starting point for constructing resolutions; combined with iterating kernels it leads to (in the P^n case) the Hilbert Syzygy theorem which bounds the length of a free resolution by ≤ n (Theorem 15.3.2).
